title: Research Journal #32 — Three Architectures, No Predetermined Winner
html:
What happens when a research project discovers that its existing software architecture has important unresolved problems, but cannot yet establish what should replace it?

That was the question facing Beyond the Light Barrier after the formal closure of our AR-1.7 Architecture Stress Audit.

As described in Research Journal #31 , the investigation had ended within its defined scope. Eight architectural findings remained open, and the audit had preserved 64 FAIL observations across the investigated variants. These observations did not represent 64 distinct architectural defects. The existing architecture had not achieved acceptance.

We had learned a great deal about what needed further investigation. But we had not yet determined what the next architecture should look like.

The newly adopted Next Architecture Exploration program, NAE-1, gave us a way to investigate that question without assuming the answer in advance.

And by October 29, three distinct architectural candidates were ready for a bounded comparison.

Three Different Ways to Organize Scientific Research

BTLB-SIM began as a scientific simulation framework, developed partly in response to our desire to investigate particle-accelerator concepts computationally without depending immediately on access to a physical accelerator.

As the project evolved, the intended framework became more general. We wanted to support different scientific applications while maintaining trustworthy execution, records, provenance, and verification.

But there is more than one way to organize those responsibilities.

NAE-1 examined three candidates.

ARCH-001 — A Common Scientific-Claim Lifecycle

The first candidate proposed organizing research around a common, governed lifecycle for scientific claims.

Different investigations could use shared vocabulary and common processes for recording, evaluating, and preserving scientific claims.

That could provide consistency across research activities.

However, it also raised a concern.

Would a common framework gradually acquire too much responsibility for deciding what scientific information meant?

A system responsible for coordinating research must not silently become the scientific authority for every investigation it coordinates.

ARCH-001 offered useful common structure, but the risk of excessive centralization needed consideration.

ARCH-002 — Evolving the Existing Architecture

The second candidate emphasized preserving and evolving the architecture already developed.

Rather than beginning with an entirely new organizing principle, ARCH-002 proposed explicit successor boundaries and versioned inheritance.

This offered an attractive possibility: preserve useful work, retain historical continuity, and change the architecture in controlled stages.

But evolution also has costs.

As components and interfaces change, the system must preserve the meaning of older records and contracts. Version management can become complicated, and scientific meaning can become entangled with the history of software interfaces.

ARCH-002 therefore offered continuity, but also raised questions about long-term complexity and architectural coupling.

ARCH-003 — Independent Scientific Records with Claim-Scoped Federation

The third candidate approached the problem differently.

ARCH-003 emphasized independently attributable scientific records and explicit relationships among them.

Rather than assuming that all investigations must pass through one common scientific-claim lifecycle, different research activities could produce records appropriate to their own scientific contexts.

Those records could then be connected, compared, or used to support subsequent claims through explicitly governed relationships.

Consider a hypothetical investigation involving a proposed gravitational effect.

One researcher might develop an analytic calculation. Another might produce a numerical simulation. A third might perform an experimental measurement.

Those activities do not automatically become equivalent simply because they address the same physical question.

Each has different assumptions, methods, limitations, and evidentiary status.

An architecture based on independent records could preserve those distinctions while allowing later investigations to establish justified relationships among them.

But ARCH-003 was not free of risks.

Independent records can become fragmented. Dependencies between investigations can remain hidden. Verification responsibilities can be shifted between components without actually being resolved.

A system that distributes scientific responsibilities must still establish who is accountable for each important decision.

ARCH-003 offered a promising direction, but it was not a proven solution.

Comparing the Alternatives Without Inventing a Winner

On October 29, the three candidates underwent a bounded architectural comparison.

The comparison examined:

  • 24 evaluation criteria
  • 72 candidate assessment rows
  • 12 noncompensable scoped gates

The gates were intended to prevent a serious deficiency in one important area from being casually offset by attractive features elsewhere.

For example, an architecture should not be considered adequate merely because it appears convenient or efficient if it cannot preserve scientific provenance or maintain necessary responsibility boundaries.

But the comparison had an important limitation.

It did not establish a numerical ranking, measured superiority, or a selected winner.

The assessment clarified the alternatives, their organizing principles, their potential benefits, and their unresolved risks.

It did not demonstrate that one architecture would be faster, easier to implement, more scientifically reliable, or more successful in actual operation.

Those claims would require additional evidence.

This distinction mattered because architectural comparisons can create an illusion of certainty.

A detailed evaluation table may look authoritative, but its conclusions are only as strong as the evidence and assumptions behind them.

The purpose of this comparison was to inform a decision—not to manufacture proof that the decision had already been made.

Why We Chose ARCH-003

Following the comparison, additional bounded inquiries and a whole-decision reassessment examined the alternatives.

On October 30, the project owner selected ARCH-003 as the architecture-development direction.

The decision reflected an engineering judgment that ARCH-003's organizing principle was worth developing further, particularly its emphasis on independently attributable scientific records and explicit relationships among claims.

This direction appeared compatible with an important principle emerging from the earlier architecture investigation:

Coordinating scientific work does not automatically confer authority to interpret its scientific meaning.

That distinction is particularly relevant to Beyond the Light Barrier.

Our research includes analytic physics, proposed computational investigations, engineering concepts, and potentially future physical experiments.

A framework that stores a simulation result must not automatically treat it as experimental evidence.

A framework that connects two records must not automatically conclude that one validates the other.

And a framework that manages a research workflow must not assume that it possesses the scientific authority to interpret every result produced within that workflow.

ARCH-003 provided a direction for investigating these responsibilities more explicitly.

But selecting it did not establish that the architecture could successfully fulfill them.

The decision was reversible.

ARCH-001 and ARCH-002 were not scientifically disproved. Neither was shown to be incapable of satisfying the project's requirements.

The selected direction could still be revised or rejected if subsequent evidence revealed unacceptable limitations.

A Decision Is Not an Implementation

There is a difference between deciding which architectural approach deserves further development and establishing that the approach works.

At the October 30 decision point, ARCH-003 had been selected as a development direction.

It had not yet received the subsequent bounded adequacy acceptance.

Its conceptual architecture had not yet been frozen.

Its detailed design had not been completed.

And no implementation had been authorized by the selection decision.

The eight inherited AR-1.7 findings remained open.

Selecting a new direction did not correct the historical problems, establish software conformance, demonstrate numerical accuracy, or validate any scientific model.

It also did not establish anything about the physical feasibility of faster-than-light communication, faster-than-light propulsion, or wormholes.

Those remain separate scientific questions requiring evidence appropriate to their claims.

Why This Matters Beyond Software Architecture

The central issue is broader than how we organize software components.

Scientific research depends on knowing what a result actually establishes.

A mathematical derivation, a numerical simulation, an independent reproduction, and a physical experiment can all contribute to an investigation.

But they do not provide interchangeable kinds of evidence.

A trustworthy research system should preserve those differences rather than blur them.

It should also preserve uncertainty, failed approaches, unresolved dependencies, and the history of how conclusions were reached.

ARCH-003 was selected as a direction for investigating how such responsibilities might be organized.

Whether it ultimately succeeds must be established through subsequent design work, implementation, verification, and appropriate scientific validation.

What Comes Next?

The October 30 decision gave NAE-1 a direction, but not a completed architecture.

The next task was to examine whether ARCH-003 could be specified coherently enough to support further development.

That required confronting the inherited AR-1.7 findings, evaluating conceptual responsibilities, and determining whether the proposed architecture contained contradictions or unresolved issues serious enough to require a different direction.

The next Research Journal entry will examine that process—and the distinction between accepting a conceptual architecture within defined limits and demonstrating that an implemented system works.

Research Reflection

There is a temptation in research and engineering to treat a decision as proof that the chosen approach was the correct one.

But a decision can be justified without being infallible.

The October 29 comparison did not produce a winner through measurement or mathematical proof.

The October 30 decision did not eliminate uncertainty.

What it accomplished was narrower, but useful: it established a documented, attributable, reversible direction for the next stage of investigation.

We did not need to pretend that the alternatives had failed in order to choose one to investigate further.

Sometimes progress means making a defensible decision while preserving the possibility that future evidence will require us to change it.

Preserved within the October 30 owner-direction package, Git commit 98ffa86d440b8edf4b841d53e0a337af47b2ffa9. Documents the three candidates, 24 criteria, 72 assessment rows, and 12 scoped gates. The comparison does not establish a ranking or selected architecture.
  3. Beyond the Light Barrier (2026). NAE-1 Owner Direction Decision v1.0. October 30, 2026. Git commit 98ffa86d440b8edf4b841d53e0a337af47b2ffa9. Records the reversible selection of ARCH-003 as the architecture-development direction and its limitations.
  4. Beyond the Light Barrier (2026). AR-1.7 Final Bounded Closure Record. October 24, 2026. Git commit cee28d7a3016223e0f28b776683a780d77fd707e, annotated tag ar17-final-closure. Documents bounded closure with unresolved architectural findings and no architecture acceptance.
  5. Beyond the Light Barrier (2026). Research Journal #31 — Closing an Investigation Without Declaring Victory . Public research chronology documenting AR-1.7 closure and NAE-1 charter adoption.
